```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(survival)
library(flexsurv)

source("R/hta_methods.R")

fmt <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
est <- function(fit) setNames(fit$res[, "est"], rownames(fit$res))

cut_year <- 3
bc <- flexsurv::bc %>%
  mutate(time3  = pmin(recyrs, cut_year),
         event3 = as.integer(censrec == 1 & recyrs <= cut_year))
stopifnot(nrow(bc) == 686, sum(bc$censrec) == 299)

dists <- c(exp = "Exponential", weibull = "Weibull", gompertz = "Gompertz",
           llogis = "Log-logistic", lnorm = "Log-normal", gengamma = "Generalised gamma")
model_colours <- c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#D55E00", "#56B4E9")
names(model_colours) <- dists
```

## Why an HTA needs more than the trial

A cost-effectiveness model needs the mean survival of patients over their
lifetime. That is the area under the whole survival curve. A trial stops long
before everyone has had the event, so the Kaplan-Meier curve ends early. The
restricted mean survival time of chapter 1 uses only the observed part.
Extrapolation means fitting a parametric model to the observed data and using
it to extend the curve.

Models that fit the trial equally well can extend it very differently, and
the choice can change the cost per quality-adjusted life year more than any
other assumption. The NICE Decision Support Unit therefore set out a
systematic process for model choice in Technical Support Document 14 (last
updated March 2013). Technical Support Document 21 (updated March 2022)
covers more flexible models for complex hazards. Extrapolation matters most
where cost-effectiveness is assessed, as at NICE. A benefit assessment such
as the German one compares effects within the observed data.

## The data and the exercise

The German Breast Cancer Study Group data hold `r nrow(bc)` patients with
node-positive breast cancer, followed for up to `r fmt(max(bc$recyrs), 1)`
years. The outcome is recurrence-free survival, with `r sum(bc$censrec)`
events. Patients are split into three prognostic groups from a published
model. Source: Sauerbrei W, Royston P. Building multivariable prognostic
and diagnostic models: transformation of the predictors by using fractional
polynomials. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A* 1999,
162, 71-94. The data ship with `{flexsurv}`.

The exercise imitates a trial that has just ended. All follow-up is cut at
`r cut_year` years, which leaves `r sum(bc$event3)` events. The models see
only these data. The later follow-up, which a real assessment would not have,
then shows how good each extrapolation was.

## Step 1. Look at the hazard before choosing a model

The log of the cumulative hazard against log time is a useful first plot. A
straight line suggests a Weibull model, which includes the exponential as a
straight line of slope 1. Parallel lines for different groups suggest
proportional hazards between them.

```{r loglog, fig.height = 4}
km_groups <- survfit(Surv(time3, event3) ~ group, data = bc)
broom::tidy(km_groups) %>%
  filter(estimate > 0, estimate < 1) %>%
  mutate(group = sub("^group=", "", strata)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(log(time), log(-log(estimate)), colour = group)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Good = "#009E73", Medium = "#E69F00", Poor = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "log(years)", y = "log(cumulative hazard)", colour = "Prognostic group") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The curves are roughly straight and parallel. A Weibull model, or a model
with proportional hazards between groups, is plausible within 3 years. The
plot cannot say what happens after 3 years.

## Step 2. Fit the standard models

Six standard models are fitted to the 3-year data, for all patients
together. The Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC, BIC) compare
their fit to the observed data, with a penalty for each extra parameter.
Lower is better. The code computes each log-likelihood by hand from the
survival and density functions, at the fitted parameters, and compares it
with `{flexsurv}`.

```{r fits}
fits <- lapply(names(dists), function(x)
  flexsurvreg(Surv(time3, event3) ~ 1, data = bc, dist = x))
names(fits) <- names(dists)

fit_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(names(dists), function(x) {
  f  <- fits[[x]]
  ll <- if (x == "gengamma") NA else param_loglik_hand(x, bc$time3, bc$event3, est(f))
  data.frame(Model = dists[[x]], Parameters = length(est(f)),
             `Log-likelihood` = round(f$loglik, 2),
             `Hand - flexsurv` = if (is.na(ll)) "" else sprintf("%.1e", ll - f$loglik),
             AIC = round(AIC(f), 1), BIC = round(BIC(f), 1), check.names = FALSE)
}))
fit_tab %>% arrange(AIC)
```

The generalised gamma fits best by AIC and BIC, then the log-normal and the
log-logistic. The exponential, with a constant hazard, fits worst. The hand
check is left blank for the generalised gamma, whose density is more
involved.

## Step 3. Extrapolate and compare with what happened next

The plot shows the Kaplan-Meier curve of the full data, including the years
the models did not see, and each model's curve extended to 10 years.

```{r extrapolation, fig.height = 5.5}
grid <- seq(0.01, 10, by = 0.01)
curves <- bind_rows(lapply(names(dists), function(x) {
  s <- summary(fits[[x]], t = grid, type = "survival", ci = FALSE)[[1]]
  data.frame(model = dists[[x]], time = s$time, surv = s$est)
})) %>% mutate(model = factor(model, levels = dists))

km_full <- survfit(Surv(recyrs, censrec) ~ 1, data = bc)
km_dat  <- data.frame(time = c(0, km_full$time), surv = c(1, km_full$surv))

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = cut_year, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey92") +
  geom_step(data = km_dat, aes(time, surv), linewidth = 1, colour = "black") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(time, surv, colour = model), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cut_year, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "Years", y = "Recurrence-free survival", colour = NULL,
       caption = paste("Black: Kaplan-Meier of the full data. Models fitted to the",
                       "first 3 years only. Shaded: data the models did not see.")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey40"))
```

```{r validation}
obs <- summary(km_full, times = c(3, 5, 7))
rmst7_km <- unname(summary(km_full, rmean = 7)$table["rmean"])

val_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(names(dists), function(x) {
  f  <- fits[[x]]
  sv <- summary(f, t = c(3, 5, 7), type = "survival", ci = FALSE)[[1]]$est
  data.frame(Model = dists[[x]], AIC = sprintf("%.1f", AIC(f)),
             `S(3 years)` = fmt(sv[1]), `S(5 years)` = fmt(sv[2]), `S(7 years)` = fmt(sv[3]),
             `RMST to 7 years` = fmt(summary(f, t = 7, type = "rmst", ci = FALSE)[[1]]$est, 2),
             `Mean to 15 years` = fmt(summary(f, t = 15, type = "rmst", ci = FALSE)[[1]]$est, 2),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
bind_rows(
  data.frame(Model = "Observed (Kaplan-Meier, full data)", AIC = "",
             `S(3 years)` = fmt(obs$surv[1]), `S(5 years)` = fmt(obs$surv[2]),
             `S(7 years)` = fmt(obs$surv[3]), `RMST to 7 years` = fmt(rmst7_km, 2),
             `Mean to 15 years` = "not observable", check.names = FALSE),
  val_tab
)
```

At 3 years every model agrees with the data, within about two percentage
points. At 7 years the predictions range from
`r fmt(min(as.numeric(val_tab[["S(7 years)"]])))` to
`r fmt(max(as.numeric(val_tab[["S(7 years)"]])))`, against an observed
`r fmt(obs$surv[3])`. The mean recurrence-free time over 15 years, the
quantity a cost-effectiveness model would use, ranges from
`r fmt(min(as.numeric(val_tab[["Mean to 15 years"]])), 2)` to
`r fmt(max(as.numeric(val_tab[["Mean to 15 years"]])), 2)` years.

Three lessons follow. First, the model with the best AIC is not the best
extrapolation here: the generalised gamma overestimates survival from year
5 on. AIC measures fit to the data the model has seen, not to the future.
Second, the exponential, which fits the first year worst, comes closest to
the observed curve after year 4, because the observed hazard levels off.
Third, the Gompertz and Weibull models, with hazards that keep rising,
predict far too many late events. The differences lie almost entirely in
the years nobody observed, and the observed tail itself rests on few
patients after year 6.

## Step 4. Look at the hazards the models assume

The extrapolated curves differ because the models assume different shapes of
hazard over time. Plotting the hazards makes the assumptions visible, so they
can be judged against clinical knowledge.

```{r hazards, fig.height = 4.5}
hz <- bind_rows(lapply(names(dists), function(x) {
  s <- summary(fits[[x]], t = grid, type = "hazard", ci = FALSE)[[1]]
  data.frame(model = dists[[x]], time = s$time, hazard = s$est)
})) %>% mutate(model = factor(model, levels = dists))

ggplot(hz, aes(time, hazard, colour = model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = cut_year, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cut_year, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Years", y = "Hazard of recurrence or death per year", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The Weibull and Gompertz hazards rise without limit. The log-normal,
log-logistic and generalised gamma hazards rise and then fall. For
recurrence after breast cancer surgery, a hazard that peaks in the first
years and then declines is the more plausible shape. That clinical argument,
not AIC alone, would decide the base case.

## What a submission would do

The usual process, as set out in TSD 14, runs as follows.

1. Check proportional hazards between the arms, for example with the
   log-cumulative hazard plot. If they hold, a model with treatment as a
   covariate is possible. If not, fit each arm separately.
2. Fit the standard models: exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic,
   log-normal and generalised gamma.
3. Compare their fit to the observed data with AIC and BIC, and by eye.
4. Judge the extrapolated part for clinical plausibility, using external
   data such as registries or longer trials, and clinical opinion.
5. Choose a base case and report plausible alternatives as scenario
   analyses.

When no standard model captures the hazard, TSD 21 describes more flexible
options: spline models, piecewise models, cure models and mixture models.
They fit the observed data better but do not remove the need to justify the
extrapolated part.

  *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A* 1999, 162, 71-94.
  As used in Royston P, Parmar MKB. Flexible parametric
  proportional-hazards and proportional-odds models for censored survival
  data. *Statistics in Medicine* 2002, 21, 2175-2197.
- NICE Decision Support Unit. Technical Support Document 14: Survival
  analysis for economic evaluations alongside clinical trials,
  extrapolation with patient-level data. Last updated March 2013.
- NICE Decision Support Unit. Technical Support Document 21: Flexible
  methods for survival analysis. Updated March 2022.
- Jackson C. flexsurv: a platform for parametric survival modeling in R.
  *Journal of Statistical Software* 2016, 70(8), 1-33.
